newsitem.title: BURMA: Rifts deep as Burma marks Union Day golden jubilee.
newsitem.headline: Rifts deep as Burma marks Union Day golden jubilee.

text.p: Burma's military rulers and the opposition led by Aung San Suu Kyi held separate events to mark the golden jubilee of Union Day on Wednesday, signalling that political divisions still run deep in the multi-ethnic nation.

Suu Kyi's National League for Democracy (NLD) party called for tripartite talks between the ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC), various ethnic groups and pro-democracy forces to build national reconciliation.

Prime Minister General Than Shwe, in an apparent reference to the Suu Kyi-led opposition and its western democracy supporters, urged ethnic groups to rise up and crush internal and external elements out to disturb Burma's progress.

About 10,000 people joined SLORC leaders at a government celebration in the People's Square in central Rangoon, while about 1,000 NLD supporters and some diplomats crowded into the grounds of Suu Kyi's lakeside residence to mark the day.
A Burmese government statement said the gathering at Suu Kyi's residence had not been not cleared by the authorities, but they had let it go ahead anyway to avoid a confrontation.

The NLD had originally said its township branch would be meeting at Suu Kyi's residence but when it became clear it was going to be on a national level, the authorities asked it to re-submit its application, the statement said.

"The NLD party ignored the injunction and rallied a mass of people... Although no proper official request was submitted to the authorities, the authorities avoided an international confrontation by allowing the ceremony to proceed," it added.

Union Day marks the February 12, 1947, agreement signed by various national races to form the Union of Burma and fulfil a condition set by the British colonial government to grant the country independence the following year.
But shortly after independence, several ethnic groups formed rebel factions and fought the Rangoon central goverment.

Amnesty International, in a report released on Wednesday, said political repression and human rights violations in Burma last year reached their highest levels since the violent state suppression of a popular uprising at the end of the 1980s.
The human rights body said more than 2,000 people were arrested in 1996 for urging human rights reform, while it said opposition party members were also attacked by organised mobs.
The SLORC described the report as "ridiculous" and propaganda for anti-Burmese organisations.

Also present at Suu Kyi's home were representatives of the Shan NLD and the Mon National Democratic Front. Burma is home to various ethnic races, including the Kachin, Kayah, Karen, Chin, Barma, Mon, Rakhine and Shan.

Than Shwe, in a message published in official media, said: "All the national brethren are urged to protect the stability and progress of the nation...to oppose and crush the internal and external elements who are disturbing and disrupting the progress of state."
He said 15 armed rebel groups had returned to the legal fold but made no mention of the Karen National Union guerrilla group, which was formed in 1948 to seek more autonomy for the Karen state.
Nobel peace laureate Suu Kyi invited various ethnic groups to meet the NLD.
"We invite the nationality groups to come and have a meeting with the NLD because we, of course, represent the people of Burma. We received the mandate in the 1990 general election," she added.
The NLD swept to victory in the election but its victory was not recognised by the SLORC.
In Bangkok, about 20 exiled Burmese students staged a brief protest in front of the Burmese embassy and demanded that the SLORC relinquish power.
